speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: asked the Minister for Manpower in the last five years, what are the statistics for persons with disabilities with regard to (i) their general employment rates, (ii) their employment rates by 10-year age groups and (iii) the main sectors employing them.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) whether he can provide an update on the progress of programmes to help companies employ and train persons with disabilities (PwDs), including the current number of companies and PwDs involved; and (b) whether there are long-term studies to monitor the effectiveness of these programmes in integrating PwDs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Would you like to take the two questions together?

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: I will take Question Nos 1 and 2 together.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Another 4.2% of PwDs in this age range were without a job and actively looking for one, translating to a resident unemployment rate of 12.9%.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The remaining two-thirds of PwDs aged 15 to 64 were outside of the labour force, with most of them citing poor health or disability as the main reason.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Member also asked for a breakdown of employment rates by age bands.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The sectors employing the most resident PwDs are Community, Social and Personal Services, Food Services, Administrative and Support Services and Manufacturing, which together account for more than half of PwD employment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Besides Mr Chong Kee Hiong, Dr Intan Mokhtar had also filed a Parliamentary Question* for the next Sitting on the effectiveness of Government schemes in helping companies or employers to hire adults with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In particular, she cited the Special Employment Credit (SEC), Open Door Programme (ODP) and Workfare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To enable more PwDs of working age to be active in the labour force, the Government provides support in several ways.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In 2012, MOM extended SEC to employers that hire Singaporeans with disabilities of all ages earning up to $4,000 a month.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: SEC provides an automatic wage offset of up to 16% of the employee’s monthly income for PwDs aged below 67, and up to 22% for PwDs aged 67 and over.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This number has increased from 2012, when SEC was paid to around 3,200 employers hiring about 5,000 Singaporeans with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers and PwDs can tap on the employment support services and programmes under the Adapt and Grow initiative.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: ODP, which is administered by SG Enable with funding support from Workforce Singapore, provides job placement and job support services for PwDs and their employers, and grants for training and job redesign.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The ODP Training Grant provides a subsidy of up to 90% of course fees to support the training of PwDs and their co-workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The ODP Job Redesign Grant provides employers with funding of up to 90% of the job redesign costs, capped at $20,000 per employee with disability, to help integrate PwDs at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Some employers and PwDs may have reservations about job fit and the suitability of the work environment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To address these concerns, Career Trial provides an opportunity for jobseekers and employers to try out each other and assess job fit through a trial.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: During the trial, which can be up to three months, jobseekers receive a training allowance from the Government.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At least 60% of these PwDs remained employed after six months.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: WIS tops up the salaries and CPF savings of lower-wage PwDs, with up to $3,600 in cash and CPF contributions annually.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: WTS provides support, such as course fee subsidies, monetary awards and training allowances, to encourage lower-wage PwDs to upgrade their skills.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Last year, more than 6,400 Singaporeans with disabilities benefited from WIS, up from more than 3,500 in 2012.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The number of Singaporeans with disabilities who benefited from WTS training also increased last year to about 860, up from about 640 in 2017.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There are also ongoing efforts to help PwDs integrate into the workforce.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Earlier this year, MOM and SG Enable launched the Job Redesign Guide for Inclusive Employers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Guide provides step-by-step information for companies on how they can redesign jobs to suit PwD workers, for instance, through changes to the workplace or working arrangements.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: SG Enable also runs disability management workshops and a biennial Inclusive Business Forum to equip employers with knowledge and skills on how to recruit PwDs and integrate them into the workforce.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Inclusive employment requires collaboration amongst the public, private and people sectors.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In March this year, the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) announced the formation of a new workgroup under the Third Enabling Masterplan to look at preparing PwDs for the future economy by enhancing access to lifelong learning opportunities and employment pathways.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The workgroup is co-chaired by Minister of State for Social and Family Development Sam Tan and Mayor Denise Phua.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The workgroup is engaging PwDs and their caregivers, social service agencies and other disability stakeholders to better understand the needs, challenges and aspirations of PwDs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The workgroup aims to release their recommendations early next year.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That is, the Ministry consolidates all the job vacancies from different employers so that PwDs know that there is a one-stop portal that they can go to, to look for employment or even training opportunities; likewise, for the employers to do so.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I would just like to clarify on the first supplementary question: is the Member asking for more schemes or just putting in place affirmative action?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As I have mentioned, today, we have the SEC which already subsidises the salaries of PwDs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Other schemes, such as ODP, help with job redesign and so forth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: From the perspective of implementing schemes, I think we are quite well resourced.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: More can still be done to encourage employers to think about having more PwDs and being more inclusive.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That is an effort that we are working quite closely with MSF and even the Ministry of Education for the Special Education schools, to see how we can make pathways more available.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That is an area that the new workgroup that I mentioned earlier would be looking into.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is a bit premature to be talking about what upcoming policies we would need to shape.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But clearly, we can do better in terms of employment outcomes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is one area we can look at.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On the second question with regard to a one-stop portal, that is something we can study.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Today, we have something like a Jobs Bank that Workforce Singapore already has.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That is one area we could potentially study.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It was reported that just five in 100 PwDs here have jobs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Back then, PwD data from our comprehensive labour force survey was not ready.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, understandably, they had patched together from different sources.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This was an underestimate, as SEC does not cover PwDs earning $4,000 and above a month.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time, there were also others who were not registered with SG Enable.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For the total number of PwDs in our population, The Straits Times applied the estimated prevalence rate from a National Council of Social Service (NCSS) survey of 2,000 persons.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is different from what we have for our comprehensive labour force survey which covers about 100,000-plus persons from 33,000 households.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, it is a lot more accurate view of what the population is.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And given the small sample survey, there is a higher margin of error in estimating the true prevalence rate.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Such a small difference in the estimated and true prevalence rate would result in a significant numerical difference in the derived PwD population.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time, The Straits Times used NCSS' estimated prevalence rate for PwDs aged 50 and over to compute the population size for PwDs aged 50 to 64.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is inaccurate as the estimate is affected by PwDs aged above 64.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For those above 64, you will find a higher prevalence of disability, not just because of conditions which you were born with, but also because of old age and so you have deterioration of health, stroke and other conditions that also add up to disability.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, if you look at some of these composites that were put together, there is a difference in the numbers that came out.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we have now used the comprehensive labour force survey which is more comprehensive.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Last year was the first year for which we have available data.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The first is, we have tracked the number of differently abled people who are employed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Do we know how long these employed people are in their employment?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: My personal experience is that I almost get a request for employment every other day at Hush TeaBar from the deaf community.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am wondering, as much as they are employed, how long do they actually stay in employment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I want to qualify that I am not asking for an employment quota for employers, but I am asking if we, as a country, is committing to a national target in terms of inclusive employment, particularly for PwDs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Certainly, from a settling in perspective, we also provide support through the Job Redesign Grant.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is not just to support the placement but also to support the education and cultural awareness education of fellow employees as well, to help them settle in.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time, it is a lot of work.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Having spoken to members and workers from SG Enable and other voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) who are doing this, there is quite a lot of work to do as well to help a PwD settle into some of the workplaces.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I hope that through greater awareness, through Members like Ms Anthea Ong and other VWOs around, we can certainly do better to bring employers on board, create awareness and help our PwDs to be more gainfully employed.
